wstep: This card describes the NCHFP recipe for fermented dill pickles with the optional garlic; the brine in this recipe contains vinegar.

akapity: Do not make fermented pickles with a reduced amount of salt.
If the pickles become soft, slimy or develop a disagreeable odor, discard them.
In the NCHFP recipe garlic is an optional ingredient: 2 cloves for each gallon of container capacity.
JarAtlas rule (cautious): NCHFP does not test more garlic or a brine without vinegar, so do not add more garlic, do not leave out the vinegar and do not change the amount of salt.

This is industrial practice, not a home recipe: in industry, brines for bulk cucumber fermentation equalize to at least 5% salt; 2% salt is the level used for cabbage and other ready-to-eat fermented vegetables.
For each gallon of container capacity, NCHFP lists 4 pounds of 4-inch pickling cucumbers, 1/2 cup of salt, 1/4 cup of 5% vinegar and 8 cups of water.
NCHFP also lists dill: 2 tablespoons of dill seed, or 4–5 heads of fresh or dry dill weed.
Add 2 cloves of garlic; the recipe also allows 2 dried red peppers or 2 teaspoons of whole mixed pickling spices, which are optional too.
Use canning or pickling salt; do not use flake salt, because its density varies.
Do not use reduced-sodium salt or salt substitutes in fermented pickles.
Penn State Extension advises vinegar of 5–7% acidity for home food preservation and advises against diluting vinegar with water unless a research-tested recipe says so.

JarAtlas rule (cautious, for readers outside the USA): use white distilled (spirit) vinegar or cider vinegar labelled 5% or 6% acidity; do not use 10% vinegar and do not dilute it with water to make 5% vinegar; add only the water the recipe lists.
Wash the cucumbers.
Cut off and discard a 1/16-inch slice from the blossom end, because it may contain softening enzymes.
Leave 1/4 inch of stem attached.
Put half of the dill and spices on the bottom of a clean container, then add the cucumbers and the rest of the dill and spices.
Dissolve the salt in the vinegar and water, pour it over the cucumbers, and add a cover and a weight.
Throughout fermentation the cucumbers must stay 1–2 inches (about 2.5–5 cm) under the brine.
At 70–75 °F (21–24 °C) fermentation takes about 3–4 weeks.
At 55–65 °F (13–18 °C) it also works, but takes 5–6 weeks.
Avoid temperatures above 80 °F (27 °C), or the pickles will become soft.
Check the container several times a week and promptly remove surface scum or mold.
Fully fermented pickles may be kept in the original container in the refrigerator for about 4–6 months, if surface scum and mold are removed regularly.
NCHFP calls canning a better way to store them.
To can them, pour the brine into a pan, heat it slowly to a boil and simmer for 5 minutes.
Fill the jars with the pickles and hot brine, leaving 1/2 inch (about 1.3 cm) of headspace.
Water-bath canning, raw pack, at 0–1000 ft (up to 300 m) above sea level takes 10 minutes for pint jars and 15 minutes for quart jars.
Above 1000 ft the food may spoil if the time is not increased.
At 1001–6000 ft (above 300 m up to 1800 m) process pints for 15 minutes and quarts for 20.
Above 6000 ft (above 1800 m) process pints for 20 minutes and quarts for 25.

Keep the water at least 1 inch (about 2.5 cm) above the jar tops during processing, and 2 inches (about 5 cm) above the jars if the processing time is over 30 minutes; if needed, add boiling water around the jars, not onto them.
Start timing only once the water is boiling.
If the water stops boiling at any time, turn the heat to its highest setting, bring the water back to a vigorous boil and time the whole process again from the beginning.

When the time is up, turn off the heat, remove the canner lid and wait 5 minutes before taking the jars out; NCHFP says this wait is not needed for food safety when USDA or University of Georgia times are used.
The card converts feet to metres and rounds the limits down, towards the longer time: 1000 ft becomes 300 m and 6000 ft becomes 1800 m.
NCHFP times are for US jar sizes: a pint holds about 473 ml and a quart about 946 ml.
JarAtlas rule (NCHFP does not test metric jars): for a jar of up to 473 ml use the pint time, and for a larger jar of up to 946 ml, for example 0.5 l or 0.9 l, use the quart time.
This NCHFP recipe gives no time for jars larger than a quart, such as 1 l, so JarAtlas recommends smaller jars.
Shortening the time or cooling jars in cold water can also lead to spoilage.
If the pickles become soft, slimy or develop a disagreeable odor, discard them.
